analysis.one_liner: Set a full-employment living-wage goal, cut work hours, and required corporations to report social and environmental impacts.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 44 cosponsors but was split across four House committees that never acted on it, and it died without a vote when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill declared that every American has a right to a decent-paying job and to housing, health care, and education, and it made full employment an explicit goal of the federal budget. It would have required publicly traded corporations to disclose their impact on workers, consumers, communities, and the environment, created a national registry of corporations convicted of breaking the law, and set up a fund to shift workers from military contracts to civilian work. It also proposed shorter work hours, triple pay for overtime, and stronger union rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and underemployed workers, who would gain from national full-employment goals that every federal agency would be obligated to pursue. Low-wage workers would gain from triple-time overtime pay, a 35-hour manufacturing workweek without any pay cut, an end to compulsory overtime, and stronger collective bargaining rights. Farm families, people needing housing or health care, and workers in defense-dependent communities facing contract terminations would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Made full employment a legal responsibility: every federal agency, including the Federal Reserve, would have to plan its policies to help all Americans exercise economic rights, and federal agencies would be barred from promoting recession or unemployment as a way to hold down wages or inflation.

Set concrete employment goals for the annual federal budget: at least 3 percent annual growth and unemployment of no more than 3 percent for adults, and required the Joint Economic Committee to issue an annual economic policy resolution with employment and poverty-reduction goals that the budget would have to follow.

Would have raised pay for hourly workers by requiring triple-time pay for hours over 40 in a week, eliminating compulsory overtime, and reducing the manufacturing and mining workweek to 35 hours with no loss in weekly wages.

Affirmed the right of all employees to organize and bargain collectively, with federal support for making that right effective, and set up a fund of at least 1 percent of annual defense spending to plan the shift of workers and communities from military contracts to civilian jobs.

Required SEC-registered corporations to disclose their impact on the environment, employees, consumers, and communities; created a computerized registry of corporations found guilty of violating federal or state law; and allowed the President to deny federal contracts to repeat offenders who showed no evidence of rehabilitation.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and the Pentagon budget, which would fund the military-to-civilian conversion fund at 1 percent of defense appropriations. Publicly traded corporations and, indirectly, all state-chartered corporations, which would bear new annual reporting duties on environmental and stakeholder impacts. Employers generally would face higher labor costs from triple-time overtime and a shorter workweek. Taxpayers ultimately fund the bill, which authorizes unspecified sums for its programs. States that failed to require reports from their chartered corporations would lose federal grants and contracts.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' with no cost estimate, so taxpayers would be committing to an open-ended price tag covering public works, conversion programs, pension-fund investment guarantees, and expanded services.

Prohibiting federal agencies from 'directly or indirectly' promoting unemployment would reach the Federal Reserve, whose monetary policy of raising interest rates to fight inflation often slows hiring; the bill would put political limits on that independent role.

The enforcement teeth are blunt: any state that had not started requiring stakeholder and environmental reports from every state-chartered corporation would lose all federal grants and contracts, a heavy compliance burden on businesses of all sizes in exchange for mostly voluntary 'recognition' incentives.

Much of the bill is aspirational. Large sections merely proclaim rights and goals rather than create programs, so for all its length the practical difference in most people's lives would likely have been smaller than its language suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's aims for workers were real: full-employment budget goals, triple-time overtime, a shorter workweek without pay cuts, and corporate accountability. But the design was weak. Its most sweeping sections were declarations without enforcement, its enforceable parts imposed heavy reporting mandates on corporations and states, its spending was authorized with no limits, and its restriction on federal agencies would have constrained the Federal Reserve's independent control of inflation. An honest supporter would acknowledge this was more a statement of principles than a workable statute, which is likely part of why it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees and then to subcommittees within two weeks, and none of them ever held a markup or vote on it before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the bill on March 10, 1999, with 33 original cosponsors, all Democrats except one Independent.

The same day, the bill was referred to four committees at once — Education and the Workforce, Budget, Armed Services, and Rules — with no lead committee designated, and on March 26 it was divided among four subcommittees of Education and the Workforce.
Forty-four members cosponsored the bill: 43 Democrats and 1 Independent. No Republican signed on at any point.
No committee ever reported the bill, no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors and large corporations came out ahead: they never faced the new disclosure requirements, the corporate-crime registry, or possible loss of federal contracts. Workers and the unemployed gained nothing, because no committee ever considered the bill.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 44 cosponsors for a full-employment and corporate accountability agenda

for.name: 43 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members such as David Bonior, Nancy Pelosi, John Conyers, and Bernie-aligned Independent support

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Split the bill across four committees with no lead committee designated, leaving it without a path to the floor

against.name: Republican chairs of the four referred committees
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees and never scheduled a markup or vote; no committee acted on it during the two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors were Democrats or the one Independent; no Republican sponsored the bill, and the Republican-run committees never took it up.

industries.note: The bill would have required a planning fund of at least 1 percent of annual defense appropriations to shift military work to civilian production, with fair reimbursement but conversion away from military contracts. Contractors whose revenue depends on programs justified by the jobs they create would lose that pipeline.

Every SEC-registered corporation would have to disclose its impact on the environment, employees, consumers, and communities in annual reports, and a national registry would track corporations found guilty of breaking the law, with the President able to deny federal contracts to repeat offenders.

Triple-time pay after 40 hours, a ban on compulsory overtime, and a 35-hour manufacturing and mining workweek with no cut in weekly pay would raise labor costs for employers, likely passed on in prices or absorbed in thinner margins.

States would have to impose annual stakeholder and environmental reporting on all state-chartered corporations to keep receiving federal grants and contracts, a compliance burden, though some firms could gain recognition awards and the bill also promised anti-monopoly protections that would help small businesses against cartels and hostile buyouts.
